claim: An effect is negligible (statistically equivalent) when its interval lies wholly inside the equivalence bounds
quote:
It may be 
easiest to think of an equivalence test as checking 
whether the entire 90% CI falls between the upper and 
lower equivalence bounds

claim: An effect is not negligible when its interval lies wholly outside the bounds
quote:
The minimal-effects test 
(b) tests if the null hypothesis that an effect falls between the lower 
equivalence bound, Δ
L, and the upper equivalence bound, Δ U, can 
be rejected.

claim: An effect is inconclusive when its interval crosses a bound
quote:
If the observed effect is neither statistically 
different from zero nor statistically equivalent, there is 
insufficient data to draw conclusions.
issue: Lakens's inconclusive case is 'neither different from zero nor equivalent'; the dissertation's case (interval crosses the bound, neither equivalence nor minimal-effects test rejects) is a sound derivation from his two tests but is not stated by him

claim: (read off cite placement) ±0.2 is a justified equivalence bound
quote:
Similarly, one might set the SESOI at a Cohen’s 
d of 0.1, which is sometimes considered a trivially small 
effect size (Maxwell, Lau, & Howard, 2015). Relying on 
a benchmark is the weakest possible justification of a 
SESOI and should be avoided.
issue: Lakens gives no ±0.2 bound and advises against benchmark bounds; the threshold rests on cohen1988statistical, cited one paragraph earlier, so the cite is not wrong, but an examiner reading Lakens could raise the benchmark caveat
